html:
The Battle of Breitenfeld was fought on 17 September 1631 at Breitenfeld, just north of Leipzig in Saxony, eastern Germany. A Swedish and Saxon army under King Gustavus Adolphus beat the army of the emperor and the Catholic League under Count Tilly. It was the first big Protestant victory of the Thirty Years' War.

For twelve years the Catholic side had won almost every battle, and the emperor seemed close to controlling all of Germany. Sweden entered the war in 1630. After Tilly's troops sacked the Protestant city of Magdeburg and invaded Saxony, its elector joined the Swedes. Tilly had about 35,000 men, drawn up in large, deep squares of pikemen. Gustavus had about 23,000 Swedes in thinner, more flexible lines, with musketeers who fired in volleys and light cannon. The 18,000 Saxons ran early in the battle. The Swedes turned their line to cover the gap, held off the cavalry attacks, then counterattacked and captured Tilly's guns. Tilly lost more than half his army.

The emperor's power in northern Germany collapsed, and Gustavus marched to the Rhine and into Bavaria. Armies across Europe copied his methods. He was killed the next year at Lützen.
